outcome: No new exact van der Waerden number was determined, but two 2026 preprints moved asymptotic bounds on how the numbers grow: Fox and Hunter proved the three-color van der Waerden numbers grow faster than any exponential function (super-exponential growth), and Campos, Fox and Schildkraut proved the long-conjectured Erdős lower bound w(k) ≥ (1−o(1))k·2^(k−1) for two-color van der Waerden numbers, extending Berlekamp's 1968 prime-case result to all k. Neither result pins down a new exact value in the table of known van der Waerden numbers; both are bounds on the general growth of these numbers.

ai.basis_quote: The coloring used to prove Theorem 1, as well as a proof of Theorem 1, were generated by a query to ChatGPT 5.6 Sol Pro. The proof we present, while drawing somewhat on the proof given by ChatGPT, was produced by the authors ... All of the writing is our own.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet is about 'the values of the Van der Waerden numbers' — i.e., the open problem of determining/bounding w(r,k) (and its multicolor generalisations), of which only nine are known exactly (the last being W(3,4)=293, Kouril 2012) and for which good asymptotic bounds are otherwise the substance of the field. Two 2026 preprints move this: (1) Fox & Hunter, 'Three-color van der Waerden numbers grow super-exponentially' (arXiv:2606.02541, submitted 2026-06-01), prove the 3-colour van der Waerden numbers w(k;3) grow faster than any exponential in k, exhibiting a 3-coloring of {1,...,2^{k·log*(k)/4}} with no monochromatic k-AP; this also resolves a related Erdős–Graham problem on canonical van der Waerden numbers. I found no mention of any AI system in this paper's abstract or text. (2) Campos, Fox & Schildkraut, 'A new lower bound for two-color van der Waerden numbers' (arXiv:2608.20824, submitted 2026-08-21), prove w(k) ≥ (1−o(1))k·2^{k−1} for all k, verifying a 1968 conjecture of Erdős and extending Berlekamp's result (which only covered k−1 prime) to all integers via a product construction over Berlekamp colorings for the prime factors. This paper contains an explicit 'AI Use' disclosure: 'The coloring used to prove Theorem 1, as well as a proof of Theorem 1, were generated by a query to ChatGPT 5.6 Sol Pro. The proof we present, while drawing somewhat on the proof given by ChatGPT, was produced by the authors ... All of the writing is our own.' By the authors' own account, the model produced both the construction and an initial proof, which the authors then reworked and wrote up themselves — this is the authors doing the mathematics that appears in the presented proof while drawing on an AI-produced starting point, which I code as `assisted` rather than `generated`: the authors state the *presented* proof (the one on which the paper — and hence the result being counted — rests) 'was produced by the authors,' distinguishing it from what ChatGPT gave them. Neither paper changes a known exact value in the numbers table, and neither settles the general open question of the numbers' precise values; both move bounds on an open problem, so status is `progress` rather than `partial` or `resolved`. I also found, via the current Wikipedia article, a 2024 result (Karki, 'U(t)-Mathazine', Summer 2024) giving a new canonical/mixed van der Waerden number w(21; 2^17,3^2) = 52 — this is a genuine new exact value within the window, but for a different (canonical, many-colour, mixed-AP-length) notion of van der Waerden number than the standard w(r,k) the bullet's statement most naturally refers to; I did not verify this source directly (could not locate the primary Mathazine article) and note it here rather than making it the basis of the record, since the two arXiv preprints are independently sufficient to establish `progress` and carry the AI-relevant finding.
competing_reading: One could argue the Campos–Fox–Schildkraut role should be coded `generated`: the abstract's closing sentence, 'It was found by ChatGPT 5.6 Sol Pro,' credits the model with finding the actual mathematical content (the coloring and a proof), which is the §6.2 test for `generated` ('the model produced the proof or counterexample and people checked it'). Against this, the body's AI Use note says the authors produced the proof they present and drew only 'somewhat' on ChatGPT's proof, i.e. their own mathematical work went into what's in the paper, not pure verification of the AI's output — closer to `assisted`. I lean `assisted` because the paper explicitly separates 'was found by ChatGPT' (the abstract, discussing origin) from 'was produced by the authors' (the AI Use section, discussing the actual presented argument), and the latter is more specific and should govern. A reader could reasonably code this `generated` instead.
what_would_settle_it: The authors' full 'AI Use' section or any accompanying blog/talk describing exactly how much of the final written proof is verbatim or close paraphrase of ChatGPT's output versus independently reconstructed — e.g. did the authors independently verify Theorem 1 from scratch after seeing the AI's claim, or did they mainly clean up and rewrite the AI's argument? Either would resolve whether this is closer to `generated` (model proof, human-checked) or `assisted` (model idea, human-proved).
